title: Limb vascular trauma and haemorrhage control
subtitle: Tourniquet, hard signs, shunt or repair

sources.title: ESVS 2025 Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Vascular Trauma

sources.org: Eastern Association for the Surgery of Trauma (EAST)
sources.title: Evaluation and management of penetrating lower extremity arterial trauma: an EAST practice management guideline

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Major trauma: assessment and initial management (NG39)

red_flags.text: Hard signs of arterial injury: pulsatile bleeding, expanding or pulsatile haematoma, palpable thrill or audible bruit, absent distal pulses, or signs of distal ischaemia.
Junctional bleeding from the groin or axilla, where a limb tourniquet cannot be applied.
Posterior knee dislocation or a displaced supracondylar fracture, even with a pulse: popliteal artery injury.
A tense, painful compartment, pain on passive stretch, or increasing analgesic need after injury or revascularisation.
A mangled limb in a shocked patient. Life comes before limb.

do_now.text: Direct firm pressure on the bleeding point, then a tourniquet applied high and tight on the limb for life-threatening haemorrhage that pressure does not control.
Tighten the tourniquet until bleeding stops and the distal pulse is gone. A loose tourniquet is a venous tourniquet and increases bleeding. Add a second one above the first if needed.
Write the time of application on the tourniquet or the patient, and hand it over at every transfer.
Give tranexamic acid as soon as possible in major haemorrhage, and activate the major haemorrhage protocol.
Junctional haemorrhage: deep wound packing with haemostatic dressing and direct pressure, or a junctional device, on the way to theatre.

assess.text: Run the primary survey first. Limb haemorrhage control sits at the very start of it, before the airway, when bleeding is catastrophic.
Look for hard and soft signs. Soft signs are a history of bleeding, a small stable haematoma, a nerve deficit next to a vessel, a diminished pulse, or a wound near a major vessel.
Measure the injured extremity index: ankle or wrist pressure of the injured limb divided by the brachial pressure of an uninjured arm.
Document neurology, soft tissue loss, fracture and contamination. These decide repair versus primary amputation, not a score alone.

investigate.text: Hard signs: straight to theatre for exploration. Imaging is optional and only if it does not delay control.
Soft signs or an injured extremity index below 0.9: CT angiography.
An index of 0.9 or more with no hard signs: arterial injury is unlikely; observe and repeat examination.
On-table angiography when the injury level is uncertain or there are several levels.

resuscitate.text: Haemostatic resuscitation with blood and products in a balanced ratio, limited crystalloid, and correction of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy.
Keep tourniquet time as short as possible. Convert to direct control in theatre rather than repeatedly loosening it in the emergency department.
Temporary intravascular shunt for damage control, or to restore flow before orthopaedic stabilisation, then definitive repair once the patient and the bone are stable.

definitive.text: Proximal and distal control through healthy tissue, then debride the injured vessel back to normal intima.
Repair by direct suture, end-to-end anastomosis, or interposition graft. Autologous vein from the uninjured leg is the preferred conduit in the limb.
Low threshold for four-compartment fasciotomy after limb arterial injury, especially with prolonged ischaemia, combined arterial and venous injury, or shock.
Ligation of a non-critical artery, or primary amputation of a non-salvageable limb, is correct damage control in an unstable patient.
Repair a major vein where the patient's state allows; ligation is acceptable in the unstable patient.

escalate.text: Trauma team leader and vascular surgeon from the first call; orthopaedic and plastic surgery together for a combined bone and soft tissue injury.
Transfer to a major trauma centre with vascular cover. Shunt or tourniquet first if transfer is long.
Critical care for reperfusion injury after prolonged ischaemia.

notes: Tourniquets save lives and rarely cost limbs when used properly. The common error is a tourniquet that is too loose, too low, or forgotten.
A palpable pulse does not exclude an arterial injury. A pulse deficit is never explained by spasm until it is imaged.
When in doubt about the compartments after revascularisation, open them.
